source: Kuhn (1962) The Structure of Scientific Revolutions, ch. VI Anomaly and the Emergence of Scientific Discoveries
finding: Kuhn's founding claim: discovery is a three-part episode. It starts with awareness of an anomaly, goes on with a more or less long exploration of the anomalous area, and ends only when the theory is adjusted so that the anomaly has become the expected. Until then the new fact is 'not quite a scientific fact at all'.
numbers: No numbers. Chapter VI of the 2nd-edition text (OCR scan, pp. 52-65).
quote: Discovery commences with the awareness of anomaly, i.e., with the recognition that nature has somehow violated the paradigm-induced expectations
limits: Narrative history, not a test. Kuhn calls the distinction between discovery of fact and invention of theory 'exceedingly artificial'. Built from a few cases (oxygen, X-rays, Leyden jar).
agent_relevance: Gives the order for S6 (impasse) and O8 (reframe): notice the violated expectation, explore around it, then change the frame until the result is expected. Detecting the anomaly is only the first step; the reframe must follow.

source: Kuhn (1962) ch. VI, the oxygen case
finding: Oxygen has no single discoverer or date. Scheele made a fairly pure sample first but published late. Priestley heated red oxide of mercury in 1774 and called the gas nitrous oxide, in 1775 called it dephlogisticated air (common air with less than its usual phlogiston). Lavoisier's 1775 work did not identify it either; the 1776-77 work moved toward seeing 'what the gas was'. Even in 1777 and to the end of his life Lavoisier held oxygen to be an atomic 'principle of acidity'.
numbers: Dates: Scheele (unpublished until later), Priestley 1774 and 1775, Lavoisier 1775-1777 and later. Principle of acidity not banished until after 1810; caloric lingered until the 1860s.
quote: discovering a new sort of phenomenon is necessarily a complex event, one which involves recognizing both that something is and what it is
limits: Historians dispute details; Kuhn's account is a stylised reconstruction. The anomaly in this case (weight gain, absorption) is only implied here; the chapter says Lavoisier 'had performed experiments that did not produce the results anticipated under the phlogiston paradigm'.
agent_relevance: Shows that seeing the gas (the data) and naming what it is (the frame) are separate steps. An agent can hold the anomalous output in hand and still label it with the old category, as Priestley did. Reframe must be an explicit step with a new label, not a rereading of the same one.

source: Kuhn (1962) ch. VI, Lavoisier vs Priestley and X-rays parallel
finding: Kuhn draws a parallel: before the red-oxide experiments, Lavoisier had run experiments that gave results the phlogiston paradigm did not predict; Roentgen's discovery began when his screen glowed when it should not. In both cases perceiving an anomaly prepared the way but was only the prelude. Neither oxygen nor X-rays appeared without more experimenting and assimilation. Priestley himself said the first hints of almost all his important discoveries came as unexpected phenomena.
numbers: Three worked examples: oxygen, X-rays (Roentgen 1895), Leyden jar. No counts.
quote: the perception that something had gone wrong was only the prelude to discovery
limits: Three cases chosen to fit the pattern; no sample of failed or ignored anomalies. The Priestley remark is quoted from Conant 1957 via Kulkarni and Simon.
agent_relevance: Supports a two-stage rule: a failed expectation triggers an exploration phase (probe the anomalous area), and only after that a model change. Do not jump from detection to answer.

source: Bruner & Postman (1949) On the perception of incongruity: a paradigm. J. Personality 18, 206-223 (as described by Kuhn 1962 ch. VI)
finding: Subjects saw playing cards at gradually longer exposures. Some cards were anomalous (red six of spades, black four of hearts). Subjects first named anomalous cards as normal, with no hesitation (a black four of hearts became a four of spades or hearts). With more exposure came hesitation and a sense that something was wrong. Then often suddenly the correct naming. A few never adjusted.
numbers: Each run ended after two successive correct identifications. At 40 times the average exposure needed for normal cards, more than 10 percent of anomalous cards were still not correctly identified (figure as told by Kuhn). Subject N and the exact exposure times were NOT read from the primary paper.
quote: the anomalous cards were almost always identified, without apparent hesitation or puzzlement, as normal
limits: I read only Kuhn's retelling, not the 1949 paper, so the N, exposure times and error rates are unverified. Kuhn uses it as 'metaphor or because it reflects the nature of the mind'. Later perception work (Brewer and Lambert 1993, cited in the 1994 paper) argues Kuhn and Hanson's perceptual examples may not support theory-ladenness; the top-down effect is strong mainly when input is weak or ambiguous.
agent_relevance: Model analogue: a model will fit an anomalous input to the nearest known category with full confidence and no flag. Confidence is not an anomaly signal; the trigger must come from a check against an independent expectation.

source: Kuhn (1962) ch. VIII The Response to Crisis
finding: Counterinstances alone never make scientists drop a paradigm. Rejecting a paradigm without a substitute is rejecting science itself. Every puzzle that normal science treats as a puzzle could be seen as a counterinstance, so the line between puzzle and counterinstance is a matter of how the scientist reads it: Copernicus, Lavoisier and Einstein saw as counterinstances what Ptolemy's, Priestley's and Lorentz's schools saw as puzzles. Crisis loosens the rules of puzzle-solving by proliferating versions of the paradigm, which lets a new paradigm emerge.
numbers: No numbers. Chapter VIII (pp. ~77-91 in the 2nd edition).
quote: To reject one paradigm without simultaneously substituting another is to reject science itself.
limits: Contested by Popperians and by Lakatos (see 03_research_programmes and 04_falsificationism). Kuhn gives no rule for when an anomaly is big enough. Claim is historical, not tested.
agent_relevance: Two design points. (1) An agent should not drop a working frame on one failure; it should drop it when it has a candidate replacement (matches G1 and G6: never abstain). (2) Whether a mismatch counts as an anomaly is a decision; a code-side counter of unresolved mismatches is a better trigger than the model's feeling.

source: Chinn & Brewer (1993) Factors that influence how people respond to anomalous data. Proc. 15th Cognitive Science Society, 318-323
finding: Proposes seven responses to anomalous data when one holds theory A: (1) ignore, (2) reject (flaws, error, fraud), (3) exclude from the theory's domain, (4) hold in abeyance, (5) accept but reinterpret to fit A, (6) accept and make a minor peripheral change to A, (7) accept and change theories. Only the last produces conceptual change. The first six are theory-preserving. Eight factors steer the choice: entrenchment of A, epistemological commitments, background knowledge, availability of an alternative theory, quality of the alternative, credibility of the data, ambiguity of the data, number of lines of evidence.
numbers: Taxonomy of 7 responses and 8 hypothesised factors. Full version is Review of Educational Research 63(1), 1-49 (1993).
quote: only the last two involve any change in theory A, and only the last produces change that can be called conceptual change
limits: The factors are hypotheses drawn from history and education studies; the paper itself tests only several of them (see a07).
agent_relevance: Best-fitting taxonomy for the impasse (S6) handler. Our agent's default response to a failed check should be audited against these seven: ignoring the output, blaming the check, narrowing the claim, deferring, reinterpreting, patching, or replacing. Code can log which one the model chose and force reject-or-reinterpret to name a test.

source: Chinn & Brewer (1993) Cogsci experiment: meteor-impact theory and anomalous data (same paper as a06)
finding: Undergraduates read about the meteor-impact theory of Cretaceous extinction, then anomalous data. People who held the theory strongly mostly discounted the data; people who preferred the alternative volcano theory mostly accepted the same data. Neither giving an alternative theory nor making the data stronger changed average ratings. Accepting the data (believing it and seeing it as inconsistent) predicted a bigger drop in belief in the theory.
numbers: N=64 undergraduates, 2x2 design (alternative theory available or not x weak or strong data), 0-10 scales. Drop in meteor-theory belief 0.97 (alternative) vs 0.72 (none), F<1. Data belief 5.4 vs 5.6 (weak vs strong), F<1. Meteor proponents rated data about 5.1 vs higher for volcano proponents, t(40)=2.48, p<.02. Accepted the data: 6 of 10 volcano proponents vs 4 of 32 meteor proponents, chi-square 7.04, p<.01. Belief change correlated -.46 with (belief x inconsistency) rating; regression F(1,63)=23.66, delta R-squared .25. Of 16 who rejected strong data, 7 attacked one of two lines of evidence and ignored the other.
quote: Subjects' evaluation of data was heavily theory-laden.
limits: Single domain, students with little stake. The null effect of an alternative theory may be because students felt no need for a theory (authors' guess). Contradicts the earlier claim, in the same paper, that a plausible alternative helps (Burbules and Linn 1988; see a09).
agent_relevance: Direct warning for G2 and G5: a model that has just argued for answer A will rate contradicting data as less credible. Data evaluation must be done blind to which answer it supports, or by code. Also: 'strong' evidence did not shift people, so adding more counter-evidence to a prompt is a weak lever.

source: Chinn & Brewer (1993) Cogsci, reasons given for rejecting data
finding: Qualitative coding of why people rejected the first anomalous datum. Five types: (a) scientists overlooked an experimental factor, (b) a specific methodological flaw, (c) more research needed, (d) the theory is so well supported that the data must be wrong, (e) the data clash with other background beliefs.
numbers: 33 subjects gave classifiable rejection reasons, grouped into 5 categories. Per-category counts were not read.
limits: Counts per category not extracted. Self-reports written by students, not process measures.
agent_relevance: Category (d), 'the theory is too well supported, so the data must be wrong', is the same move as a model trusting its first answer over a failing test. A checklist of these five excuses can be used by the program to ask for a concrete test before any dismissal is accepted (G2).

source: Burbules & Linn (1988), Stavy (1991), Samarapungavan (1992) as reported in Chinn & Brewer (1993) Cogsci
finding: Reported boundary conditions on anomaly responses. Burbules and Linn: adolescents kept a wrong displacement theory after anomalous data, but changed once told the correct principle (an alternative was needed). Stavy: students resisted mass conservation after seeing colourless acetone boil, but accepted it after seeing blue iodine gas stay in the flask (unambiguous data works). Samarapungavan: first graders prefer theories with wider scope and more accuracy.
numbers: No sample sizes read; second-hand report.
limits: Second-hand, not opened. Burbules and Linn support 'alternative theory needed'; Chinn and Brewer's own experiment (a07) did not replicate that with undergraduates, so the alternative-theory effect is mixed.
agent_relevance: Two practical levers: make the anomalous output unambiguous (print the failing value, not a summary) and offer a concrete rival frame before asking the model to give up the old one.

source: Brewer & Chinn (1994) The theory-ladenness of data: an experimental demonstration. Proc. 16th Cogsci, 61-65
finding: Students first read a strong case for either warm-blooded or cold-blooded dinosaurs, or a neutral control. All then rated the same piece of data. The identical data were rated about 2 points less believable when they contradicted the theory the person had read than when they agreed. The whole effect came from the inconsistent group dropping below the control; consistent data were not boosted above control.
numbers: N=72 undergraduates, 24 per condition, fully counterbalanced. Initial theory belief (cold minus warm rating): warm group -5.5, cold group 5.9, control 1.5. Belief in data (0-10): consistent 8.0, inconsistent 6.0, control 7.8; ANOVA F(2,66)=7.292, p<.001; inconsistent vs consistent p<.05. Rated consistency of data with the theory fell modestly for inconsistent data but not reliably (p>.08). Presentation style (textbook vs experiment report) had little effect.
quote: individuals will tend to be critical of data that is inconsistent with their current theoretical beliefs
limits: Short reading passages, one domain, a theory the students had known for about 10 minutes. Authors note a moderate view of theory-ladenness: top-down effects are large when input is weak or ambiguous. Related earlier work cited: Lord, Ross and Lepper 1979 (capital punishment studies), Mahoney 1977 (reviewers), Pickering and Monts 1982 (over half of chemistry students rejected their own anomalous data) - not opened.
agent_relevance: The cleanest human number for our design: about 2 of 10 scale points of devaluation for data that goes against a just-adopted position. For an LLM that has just produced a chain of reasoning for answer A, expect the same direction; test it in our harness by scoring identical evidence under different prior commitments.

source: Dunbar (1995/1997) How scientists think: on-line creativity and conceptual change in science (in vivo study of molecular biology labs)
finding: Real scientists, unlike students in 2-4-6 type tasks, attend to unexpected findings. At four weekly lab meetings of one lab, unexpected results were common and drew much more theory-building than expected results. The group also paid more attention to them.
numbers: 4 lab meetings, 6 experiments, 70 conditions: 22 expected, 18 unexpected, 30 exploratory findings. Reasoning blocks (table as extracted): theory-building 33 for expected vs 161 for unexpected; explaining away 9 vs 18. Group interactions: 23 for expected vs 176 for unexpected. Of 18 unexpected, 8 were consistent with the hypothesis (effect size surprising) and 10 inconsistent (different kind of outcome). New hypotheses followed 4 of 8 consistent and 8 of 10 inconsistent unexpected findings.
limits: One lab, four meetings, coded by two coders, tiny counts, no inferential tests reported. The column alignment of the reasoning-block table in the extracted text is slightly uncertain. Dunbar himself notes that the lab studied was one with many unexpected results.
agent_relevance: Human labs treat about a quarter of results as surprising and spend most reasoning on them. Evidence that following up surprises is a normal, productive habit, not a bias. In our loop the follow-up should be triggered by a code-detected mismatch and given extra budget.

source: Dunbar (1995/1997) same chapter, when unexpected findings are ignored
finding: Attention to a surprise depends on timing and on what it contradicts. Early in a project, a surprise that hits only an auxiliary hypothesis is ignored. Early surprise against a core assumption of the field is pursued. Late in a project, scientists attend to it either way. Dunbar says students in psychology tasks sit exactly in the ignore cell (early, non-core), so the match to scientists holds only in restricted conditions. Experts have built heuristics from many encounters with surprise.
numbers: Described as 'new analyses' with no counts in this chapter.
quote: it is only under very restricted circumstances that we see a similarity between the subjects and the scientists
limits: No numbers given; claim is a summary of unpublished analyses. Relation to Dunbar's 1993 concept-discovery study (subjects ignoring unexpected results) taken from this chapter's text only.
agent_relevance: Gives a policy table for S6: the same mismatch should get different weight depending on whether it hits a core claim or a helper assumption, and on how far into the budget we are. A short mismatch-classification step in code (core vs auxiliary) is cheap.

source: Kulkarni & Simon (1988/1990) The processes of scientific discovery: the strategy of experimentation (KEKADA); read as NASA TR FIA-90-09-24-02 'Experimentation in Machine Discovery'
finding: KEKADA is an OPS5 production system modelling Hans Krebs's work on urea synthesis. It attaches an expectation to every experiment (for example, urea at 2 to 10 units). If a result violates the expectation it is flagged as a surprise, the system drops its current plan and recurses on the surprise, building new hypotheses and experiments about it. This is depth-first search with no backtracking that is easily 'distracted' by surprises.
numbers: Run on one historical case (ornithine produces ammonia in kidney slices). Illustrative expectation: urea 2-10 units, result 20. Program structure: each strategy has three parts (hypothesis generators, experiment proposers, experiment evaluators). Hypotheses are dropped after more than 3 negative instances (as stated for one strategy).
quote: KEKADA forgets its previous goals and attends entirely to the new phenomenon
limits: One reconstructed case; the surprises in later steps were supplied by the user typing results, not by a real lab. Rule-based, hand-written domain knowledge. Results sit inside the historical record, so hindsight is possible. Heuristics were extracted from Holmes's study of Krebs's notebooks.
agent_relevance: The closest formal model of the S6 trigger: write an expected outcome before each test, compare in code, switch focus on violation. Matches EvoSCM's pre-committed predictions (a21). Its 'forget previous goals' rule is the opposite of our G1 caution, so we must cap it with a budget.

source: Kulkarni & Simon (1988/1990) KEKADA strategies for a surprise
finding: Five fixed strategies for handling a surprise: (1) try to magnify it by changing apparatus variables, (2) divide and conquer, (3) assess its scope using taxonomies (does it hold for other members of the class), (4) find the relevant factors by dropping variables, (5) look for similar phenomena elsewhere. Worked run: ornithine yields ammonia in kidney, other amino acids do too (general deamination), then arsenite unexpectedly increases ammonia and keto acid from glutamic acid, then the system finds that glutamic acid combines with ammonia to give glutamine.
numbers: Three stages in the run, five knowledge states S1-S5. Outputs: deamination happens by oxidation in kidney, not liver as assumed; deamination rates for several amino acids; glutamine reaction found. Class test: a class with 3 or more negative instances inactivates the hypothesis.
quote: The basic source of KEKADA's power was its ability to create a small number of good hypotheses and experiments and to focus on surprises.
limits: Only worked example is hand-driven. Not compared with any baseline. A surprise inside a surprise is handled by recursion without a depth limit in the text.
agent_relevance: Gives a ready list of anomaly-handling moves for an operator: magnify, bisect, scope, factor-drop, find analogues. These are cheaper than a free-form 'rethink' and can be offered as O8 sub-moves, each producing a code-checkable experiment.

source: Kulkarni & Simon (1990 TR) KEKADA task definition: surprise detection versus given surprise
finding: KEKADA's definition of the task fits Kuhn's first stage: given a surprising phenomenon and a set of domain facts, carry out an experimentation program and use the results to refine the theory step by step. Unlike two peer programs (Karp 1990, Rajamoney 1990), KEKADA detects the surprise itself rather than being handed it.
numbers: No numbers.
quote: KEKADA is capable of detecting surprising phenomena and using these surprises to guide its attempts to revise the domain theory
limits: Detection works only because expectations were hand-written for each experiment type.
agent_relevance: Makes clear that detection needs an explicit expectation. For an LLM agent: have the model state a numeric or categorical prediction before running code, store it, and let the program do the comparison.

source: Darden (1991) Theory Change in Science; Darden (1992/2006) Strategies for anomaly resolution (Cognitive Models of Science; Reasoning in Biological Discoveries ch. 9)
finding: Darden frames anomaly resolution as parallel to diagnosis and redesign: first localise the fault in the theory (which component produced the wrong prediction), then redesign that component. Strategies sit between minor repair and abandoning the theory. Seen in the history of genetics.
numbers: None read; I only saw a search summary of the chapter, not the text.
limits: Not opened. Strategy names (for example localisation, monster-barring) are NOT confirmed here; a search did not return them.
agent_relevance: The diagnose-then-redesign order is the same as our G2 (revise only from real output, locate the failing step first). Worth opening in angle B or C; the model-based diagnosis subfield (Diagnosability, Readings in model-based diagnosis) overlaps and is covered there.

source: Wiemann, Smith, Melchior et al. (2026) DiscoverPhysics: Benchmarking LLMs for Out-of-the-Box Scientific Thinking, arXiv 2605.26087v2
finding: An LLM agent must find the law of motion in 22 simulated worlds whose physics deviates from ours (screened or fractional gravity, hidden dark-matter-like sources, non-coordinate-free physics, time-varying forces). It designs several rounds of experiments, then submits an explanation and code. The strongest agents pass only about half of the worlds and consistently fail on worlds with latent structure. Failure is mainly too little experimentation. Good prediction error did not guarantee a good explanation.
numbers: 22 worlds, 11 frontier models, 5 seeds per world. A world is passed if normalised trajectory MSE is below 0.1 (plus explanation criteria stated in the paper). Best models claude-opus-4-7 and gpt-5.5 pass about half; the proprietary pass@k row that appears to be the best model runs 26.4, 36.8, 43.1, 47.2, 50.0 percent for k=1..5 (row labels are scrambled in the PDF text). gpt-oss-120b and claude-haiku-4-5 sit near zero. claude-opus-4-7 improved monotonically with round budget on guided experiments; gpt-5.5 did not.
quote: strongest agents pass only half of the worlds and consistently fail on those where latent structure must be uncovered
limits: Explanation score is LLM-judged; authors flag possible Claude-on-Claude favouritism. API default sampling, mid reasoning effort. The table's row labels were scrambled in the text I read, so the model-to-number mapping is partly inferred. Not a test of anomaly triggers specifically.
agent_relevance: The failing worlds are those where a model must posit something unseen (dark matter) to explain an anomalous acceleration, i.e. the Kuhn move from 'my law is off' to 'my ontology is incomplete'. Evidence that O8-style reframing, not more fitting, is where frontier models still fail.

source: Wiemann et al. (2026) DiscoverPhysics, dark-matter world failure example (Appendix E.6)
finding: In the dark-matter world, GPT-5.5 as agent with 16 rounds fitted a central trap plus softened power-law forces and a 'rigidly evolving background'. It never proposed hidden sources, so the anomalous accelerations were explained by an extra smooth term. The judge scored the explanation 2.
numbers: Budget 16 experiment rounds; explanation score 2 (scale as defined in the paper's rubric, not read in full). One world, one run.
quote: The student misses the key structural feature of hidden dark-matter particles causing anomalous accelerations.
limits: Single qualitative example. Judge is an LLM. Not an average.
agent_relevance: Textbook case of Chinn and Brewer response 5/6: accept the anomaly and patch the existing model rather than change the ontology. A test case for our impasse detector: residuals that stay structured after a good fit should trigger 'add a latent object' as a named reframe operator.

source: Zhao, Li, Deng et al. (2026) EvoSCM: Scientific Belief Revision Through Causal Model Evolution and Experimentation, arXiv 2609.01526v2
finding: EvoSCM keeps a population of structural causal model hypotheses, makes each commit to predictions before experiments, picks experiments that separate rivals, and when observations contradict predictions turns the discrepancy into a correction rule that drives revision of dependencies, latent factors, mechanisms or parameters. On DiscoverPhysics it beats baselines by a wide margin.
numbers: GPT-5.5: explanation score 51.64% baseline vs 75.09% EvoSCM; pass@1 7.27% vs 56.36%; pass@5 27.27% vs 63.64%; normalised MSE 2.83e-2 vs 2.77e-4; episodes 2,206 vs 1,685. GPT-5.4: explanation 39.80% vs 65.30%; pass@1 1.86% vs 38.08%. Other methods (GEPA, ReasoningBank, ModelSMC, PiEvo) did not clearly beat the baseline (pass@1 0 to 10.91% for GPT-5.5).
limits: Authors' own benchmark choice and metric; the DiscoverPhysics judge is an LLM. Table was read from extracted text; columns assumed to be explanation, norm MSE, pass@1..5, episodes. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Closest 2026 LLM implementation of the anomaly-to-revision loop. Supports G2 (revise from the actual discrepancy) and G5 (code selects among competing hypotheses). Numbers are large enough to justify a small pilot in our harness.

source: Zhao et al. (2026) EvoSCM ablations (Tables 5, 6 and 11)
finding: Removing parts of the loop shows which matters. Replacing structured hypotheses with free text, or experiments with random choice, cost about 27 points; free-form revision cost about 4; removing pre-committed predictions caused a notable decline because the agent can rationalise any observation after the fact. Removing the induction of correction rules caused a moderate decline. One hypothesis is much worse than several.
numbers: Explanation score on DiscoverPhysics (GPT-5.5): full 75.09%; w/o SCM (free-form text hypotheses) 48.18%; w/o discriminative action (random) 47.45%; w/o structured revision 70.73%. Population size K=1 63.27%, K=4 74.86%, K=6 75.09%, K=8 75.01%. The pre-commitment and induction ablation numbers are in Table 11 and were not read.
quote: the agent can rationalize any observation post-hoc, weakening the discrepancy signal that drives revision
limits: Ablations are from the authors, one benchmark, single configuration. Cannot separate the effect of structure from extra prompting tokens.
agent_relevance: Strong support for pre-committed predictions as the anomaly detector: without a commitment there is no anomaly. Also supports keeping at least 3-4 rival hypotheses alive (cf. G4 on correlated samples: diversity must come from different hypotheses, not repeated sampling).

source: Zhao et al. (2026) EvoSCM transfer (Table 4)
finding: A revised causal model written down by one model can be given to a weaker model and helps it. The better the source model, the bigger the gain.
numbers: Qwen3.6 on DiscoverPhysics, explanation score: baseline 30.73%; with its own SCM 48.91%; with a GPT-5.4 SCM 57.64%; with GPT-5.5 SCM 62.55%; with the strongest named SCM 74.00% (pass@5 63.64% vs 0.00% baseline).
limits: Transfer inside one benchmark; the SCM may encode world-specific facts, so it transfers answers not just skill.
agent_relevance: Suggests the reframed model is an artefact worth saving between steps or runs, but it is also partly leakage of the answer. Treat as a reason to store the current best model as a code-readable object, not as a general skill claim.

source: Agarwal, Majumder, ... Sabharwal, Clark (2025) AutoDiscovery: Open-ended Scientific Discovery via Bayesian Surprise, NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2507.00310v3
finding: Uses the size of belief change as the exploration reward. The LLM's prior belief that a hypothesis is true is compared with its posterior after seeing experiment results; surprise is the KL divergence, counted as a 'surprisal' only if the belief flips across 0.5. Monte Carlo tree search uses this reward. It finds more surprising discoveries than repeated sampling, linear, greedy tree and beam baselines.
numbers: 21 datasets (DiscoveryBench, BLADE, SEA-AD), budget 500 hypotheses per run, GPT-4o discovery agent. 5 to 29 percent more surprisals than competitors. Human check: 1,620 LLM-surprisal hypotheses rated by 3 STEM MS/PhD annotators; two-thirds of discoveries surprising to domain experts; Bayesian-surprise correlation with human surprisal 0.67 (95% CI 0.63 to 0.71, 10,000 bootstrap resamples); the next-best automatic reward was 0.46 lower.
limits: Surprise is measured from the LLM's own prior and posterior, so a poorly calibrated prior produces false surprises. Counted over data analysis, not physical anomalies. 'Surprising' does not mean true or useful.
agent_relevance: Gives an operational impasse signal: elicit a prior probability before the check, elicit it again after, and let code flag a flip across 0.5. Beware: models' stated priors are noisy (see Calibration and overconfidence subfield, run in parallel), so use as a hint only (G1, G4).

source: Zheng, Tam, Nguyen, ... See (2026) NewtonBench: Benchmarking Generalizable Scientific Law Discovery in LLM Agents, ICLR 2026, arXiv 2510.07172v3
finding: Takes 12 canonical physics laws and shifts them (counterfactual law shifts) so memory cannot answer; agent must probe a simulated system interactively. Reasoning models do much better than non-thinking models, but all degrade sharply when the law is more complex or the system noisier.
numbers: 324 tasks over 12 physics domains, 108 shifted laws in 3 model systems, 11 LLMs. Overall symbolic accuracy: GPT-5 75.9%, Gemini-2.5-pro 65.4%; non-thinking models (GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-V3) below 10%; most reasoning models 30-80%. Hardest setting: GPT-5 40.3%, Gemini-2.5-pro 16.7%, all others below 6%. Easy setting 70-100% for reasoning models.
limits: Final answer is a symbolic equation, checked against a canonical form; no explicit anomaly trigger is tested. Noise sensitivity was described as extreme but figures not extracted.
agent_relevance: The 'shifted law' design is a model of Kuhnian anomaly: the data contradict a memorised law. Frontier models still lose most of their accuracy when the memorised frame must be replaced, supporting the need for a deliberate reframe step.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) NewtonBench section 4.5 code interpreter paradox
finding: Giving a code interpreter helps weak models but hurts strong ones. The cause is traced to an early shift from exploration to exploitation: the strong model fits locally and stops looking for the globally correct law. Exploration tokens (such as 'What if', 'Alternatively') dropped sharply for Gemini-2.5-flash when code budget went from 0 to 1, but not for Qwen-3-235b.
numbers: Weak models (symbolic accuracy below 40%) gain from the tool; stronger models (40% or above) lose slightly. Performance change is largest going from code budget 0 to 1, four models tested. Exploration rate = share of exploration tokens among exploration plus exploitation tokens.
quote: premature shift from exploration to exploitation
limits: Token-counting proxy for exploration; only two models with accessible reasoning traces; 'slight' degradation. Figure values not extracted.
agent_relevance: Warning for O8: a tool that makes local fitting easy can suppress the very reframing we want. After a good-looking fit, the program should check for structured residuals before accepting (G3) and keep an explicit 'alternative frame' step.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: A Virtual Environment for Developing and Evaluating Automated Scientific Discovery Agents, arXiv 2406.06769
finding: A text-and-grid virtual lab with 120 tasks across 8 topics and 3 difficulty levels. Agents must form hypotheses, run experiments, analyse results, and act (for example, find why colonists on Planet X get sick, or which plants need which nutrients). Baseline GPT-4o agents (ReAct, Plan-and-Execute, Hypothesizer) mostly fail; humans do much better. The paper states the agents lack the capacity for end-to-end discovery, though they do well on unit-test parts such as measuring.
numbers: 120 tasks. Best discovery agent, ReAct: 38% of easy and 18% of challenge tasks completed. Best at finding explanatory knowledge, Hypothesizer: 34% of gold knowledge on easy, 8% on challenge. Unit tests: completion in the 60%+ range. Expert humans (up to 11 per seed, 16 tasks): average completion 66%, 11 of 16 tasks above 60%, knowledge 55%.
quote: current agents are competent at many of the components of scientific discovery
limits: GPT-4o era agents; later models may differ. There is almost no analysis of anomalies as such (the word appears only inside a task about identifying an anomalous species). Humans sometimes brute-forced answers.
agent_relevance: Reference baseline for how bad agents were at full discovery in 2024 and a place to test an impasse-then-reframe scaffold; the gap between unit-test and end-to-end scores points to missing control logic, which is what S6 and O8 add.

source: Chinn & Brewer (1993) The role of anomalous data in knowledge acquisition: a theoretical framework and implications for science instruction. Review of Educational Research 63(1), 1-49
finding: Full-length source of the seven-response taxonomy, using history of science and student studies. A search summary says that only one response is real conceptual change; the rest keep the old theory. Full text could not be opened (HTTP 403 on the repository PDF).

source: Kuhn (1962) ch. VIII, the proliferation and loosening of rules
finding: Kuhn says the difference between normal science and a science in crisis is not that the first meets no counterinstances. Every paradigm leaves puzzles unsolved. Crisis is the state where scientists keep proposing varied versions of the paradigm, which loosens the rules of puzzle solving, and a new paradigm can then emerge. A crisis does not by itself turn a puzzle into a counterinstance; there is no sharp dividing line.
numbers: No numbers.
quote: by proliferating versions of the paradigm, crisis loosens the rules of normal puzzle-solving
limits: A philosophical claim. Kuhn gives no measure of when puzzle becomes crisis. Critics (Lakatos, Popper) disagree on how decisive anomalies are; see subfields 03 and 04.
agent_relevance: Suggests an observable crisis signature for S6: many different patched versions of the same approach, none passing. A code counter of 'distinct failed variants of one method' is a measurable trigger for O8 that does not need the model's opinion.

source: Cross-source comparison: KEKADA (a13), Chinn & Brewer (a07), Dunbar (a11)
finding: The three bodies of work disagree on the default. KEKADA assumes a surprise is followed up at once. Chinn and Brewer's students mostly explained the anomaly away (only 4 of 32 strong-theory holders accepted the data). Dunbar's scientists followed up most unexpected inconsistent findings (8 of 10 gave new hypotheses). The difference is who the people are, how large the stake is, and whether the surprise hits a core or auxiliary belief.
numbers: 4 of 32 vs 6 of 10 data acceptance (Chinn and Brewer, a07); 8 of 10 inconsistent unexpected findings leading to new hypotheses (Dunbar, a11).
limits: Synthesis across different tasks; the three groups differ in expertise and stake, so a direct comparison is unsafe.
agent_relevance: Our agent behaves like a novice with a strong prior: assume the default response is explain-away, and add scaffolding (pre-committed prediction, forced test of any dismissal) to push it toward the scientist pattern.

source: Kuhn (1962) ch. VI, the Leyden jar and resistance to the anomalous
finding: Kuhn's third discovery case: the Leyden jar emerged from experiments on an anomalous electrical effect, and the same experiments forced a major revision of the fluid theory of electricity, giving the first full electrical paradigm. He lists the common features of discoveries that bring new kinds of phenomena: prior awareness of anomaly, gradual and simultaneous emergence of observational and conceptual recognition, and a consequent change of paradigm categories, often with resistance.
numbers: No numbers. Cites Cohen 1956 and Whittaker for the history.
quote: the gradual and simultaneous emergence of both observational and conceptual recognition
limits: Cases picked to fit; no base rate of anomalies that led nowhere.
agent_relevance: Reminds that noticing and reframing proceed together in one loop: each new probing result both sharpens the anomaly and the candidate frame. A loop of probe-then-reframe, not a single reframing call.

source: Kuhn (1962) ch. VI, normal science makes anomalies visible
finding: Kuhn's explanation of why rigid expert practice still produces surprises: a developed paradigm builds precise instruments and tight expectations, so a result that departs from them stands out. Novelty emerges mainly for the person who knows with precision what to expect. This is a cost (restriction of vision and resistance) and a benefit (detail and precision of observation-theory match).
numbers: No numbers.
limits: OCR scan; no direct quote kept. Paraphrase of the passage that ends chapter VI section on normal science.
agent_relevance: Supports the design rule that anomaly detection needs a sharp expectation first. A vague plan gives no anomaly. Make the agent write a precise expected value or pattern before each check (G3).
